Berlin’s Pride Festival: One Killed, 30 Injured

🔤🔤🔤🔤1️⃣

A man suspected of driving a van into a crowd near Berlin’s Pride festival then going on a knife rampage in an Islamist terror attack has been shot dead by police, German officials have said.

Police confirmed on Sunday evening that the chief suspect had been shot dead, reportedly during an operation at an allotment garden complex ⁠in the capital’s Spandau district.

One woman was killed on Saturday evening and 30 others were severely injured after a man drove a rented minivan into a crowd of pedestrians, then attacked people with what appeared to be a machete. The attack took place in the Tiergarten park near the Brandenburg Gate at about 10pm local time on Saturday, close to one of Europe’s biggest LGBTQ+ celebrations.

The attack forced organisers to cut short one of Europe’s largest Pride events and came as Germany remained on edge after a series of deadly vehicle and knife attacks.

The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, named the chief suspect as 21-year-old Abdul Ballout. “We are dealing ​here with ‌a suspected ‌perpetrator, who had previously drawn attention ‌to himself through a high volume of criminal offences, radicalisation and affiliation with the Islamist scene,” he told ‌a press conference near the site of the attack. 

He said Ballout had a criminal conviction and had been sentenced as a juvenile to a year and 10 months in prison, but that the sentence had been suspended.

German media reported that Ballout, a German national with Lebanese roots, was a supporter of Islamic State and last year travelled to the Middle East in a failed attempt to join the group. He was then convicted in Germany of “preparing a serious act of subversive violence”, the news outlets Bild and Der Spiegel reported.

🔊 Iran’s envoy to Russia says Ukraine-hit vessel carried no military cargo

📌 Moscow, IRNA – Iran’s ambassador to Russia has condemned a recent drone attack by Ukraine against an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea as a “criminal act”, saying the vessel was fully civilian, carrying no military cargo.

Kazem Jalali told IRNA on Monday that one Iranian national was killed in the attack and several others were injured. He offered condolences to the family of the victim.
​
Jalali said Iran’s consulate general in the Russian city of Astrakhan worked closely with Russian authorities after the attack to facilitate the swift evacuation of Iranian crew members from the area.
​
He said the incident was the main subject of a telephone conversation on Sunday between Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his Russian counterpart Sergei Lavrov. According to Jalali, Araghchi said Iran reserved the right to respond to the attack, and that any decision on further action would be taken by the country’s leadership.
​
The ambassador said the Anna was anchored about five kilometers from the entrance to the Volga River when it was targeted by a Ukrainian drone while waiting for stormy weather to subside before continuing its voyage.
​
Responding to a question about whether Russia should retaliate because the strike took place in its territorial waters, Jalali said such an expectation was justified, adding that Iran expected Russia, as a friendly country, to give a serious response to the “criminal” attack.

The Strait of Zero: Hormuz's Perfect Shutout

Six ships tried to cross Hormuz overnight. Zero made it through. One had "an incident" — Iranian state media's polite word for a mystery blast. Five just turned around.

"Last night, six vessels that attempted to transit through a route other than the designated one were stopped by the IRGC Navy with warning shots and turned back," Iranian state television announced. Translation: Tehran runs the toll booth now. Payment is fear, not cash.

Down in the Red Sea, the Houthis run their own franchise. Spokesman Yahya Saree confirmed strikes on Aramco sites in Jizan and Yanbu. 

Consider it a courtesy call before Saudi crude learns it isn't welcome here either. 

The numbers back him up. Kpler data cited by Reuters shows just eleven vessels crossed Bab el-Mandeb on Sunday — the lowest count in months. 

Fewer than ten ships a day squeezed through Hormuz all weekend. Two chokepoints. One memo: nobody guarantees your barrel gets home.

Greece's Patriot battery earned its paycheck too, shooting down two ballistic missiles aimed at Yanbu's refineries on Saturday. Count it a rare win, if "someone else's air defense saved our oil" qualifies as national security. 

Satellite trackers cited by Iranian outlets claim Kuwait's Al-Ahmadi and Saudi's Al-Jubail terminals are running dry. Tankers are vanishing from the docks like nobody wants to be caught holding the barrel when the music stops.

Throw in unconfirmed chatter about a suicide-drone hit on Aramco's Buqayq complex, and you've got a siege nobody declared and everybody enforces. 

Iran's press keeps demanding the blockade be broken. Funny, since the only ships not moving are the ones flying flags Tehran doesn't like.

So who's actually choking off the oil — the ayatollahs playing traffic cop, or the tankers too scared to test the theory?
